summary: Explains which documents make up the complete Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS), an abstract algorithm for applying dynamically retrieved string transformation rules to an application-unique string. Together with RFCs 3402 through 3404, it replaces RFCs 2168 and 2915 and updates RFC 2276.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3401 explains which documents together define the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS). DDDS applies rules retrieved from a database to a unique string until it reaches a final result.

questions: what is the dynamic delegation discovery system
subtitle: The document map for the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System.

tldr.problem: The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System is described across several documents, and readers need to know how the parts fit together.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3401 identifies the core algorithm document, application documents that give the algorithm a purpose, and database documents that store its rules.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3401 and RFCs 3402 through 3404 obsolete RFCs 2168 and 2915 and update RFC 2276.

today: RFC 3401 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Together with RFCs 3402 through 3404, it obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915 and updates RFC 2276.

sections.title: What DDDS Does
sections.content:
DDDS maps an application-specific unique string to data in a DDDS Database. It repeatedly applies string transformation rules until it reaches a terminal condition. RFC 3401 is an overview that lists the documents making up the complete specification.

The RFC is intended for people implementing or studying the generic algorithm, URI resolution, ENUM telephone-number resolution, or the NAPTR DNS resource record. It warns that reading only one document in the series can cause misunderstandings and interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: DDDS starts with a unique string, looks up a rule, and applies the rule to find the next value. RFC 3401 identifies the documents needed to understand that process.

sections.title: The Algorithm and the Core Documents
sections.content:
RFC 3402 defines the generic algorithm, its vocabulary, and requirements for applications and databases. The algorithm by itself does not say what task to perform or where to store its rules.

Application documents provide the task-specific details. DDDS Database documents define how a database works, including key and rule formats, lookup, rule insertion, and collision avoidance. Applications and database specifications are outside the DDDS core specification, but an implementation needs both.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm gives general steps. An application says what those steps should accomplish, and a database specification explains where and how the rules are stored.

sections.title: What an Application Defines
sections.content:
An Application specification gives the concrete details needed to use DDDS. It defines the Application Unique String, the First Well Known Rule that starts the process, the valid databases, and the expected final output.

The RFC names two application examples. RFC 2916 maps E.164 telephone numbers to service endpoints such as SIP or email. RFC 3404 describes an application for resolving URIs to endpoints or resolvers that can provide further information.
sections.plainLanguage: An application specifies the starting string, the first rule, which databases can be used, and what final result is expected. The RFC gives telephone-number and URI resolution as examples.

sections.title: DDDS Databases
sections.content:
Every DDDS Application must use a DDDS Database. A database specification defines its operation, the formats of its keys and rules, how a key is looked up, how rules are inserted, and how collisions are avoided.

A database cannot be used on its own; at least one application must use it. A database may support multiple applications, and an application may use only selected databases. Compliance therefore depends on the combination of an application specification and a database specification. RFC 3403 specifies the DNS database and the NAPTR DNS resource record.
sections.plainLanguage: A DDDS database stores rules for an application. To know whether a system follows DDDS, consider both the application and database specifications it uses.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Known security issues related to an algorithm or database must be described in its specification. New database types and algorithms require security review, and their security considerations should continue to be evaluated.

RFC 3401 creates no new IANA requirements. Other documents in the series do have IANA considerations, so the RFC asks the IANA to review those documents for the complete set of registries and requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Specifications for new algorithms and databases must describe known security risks and receive security review. RFC 3401 itself adds no IANA requirements.

viz.caption: THE THREE DOCUMENT ROLES IN DDDS

layers.label: Application
layers.detail: Defines the unique string, starting rule, valid databases, and final output.

layers.label: DDDS algorithm
layers.detail: Defines the vocabulary, algorithm, and requirements. RFC 3402.

layers.label: Database
layers.detail: Defines how keys and rules are stored, found, and added.
